Senses.Explanation: Literally, a root of life: in Chan records, the hold described as being cut, broken, or gathered up. The phrase occurs 829 times in 226 allowlisted texts. Luyuan spreads his hand and says that the life-roots of all the old masters and senior monks are “all here” (all the old masters and senior monks' life-roots are all here). Hui'an Miguang supplies the corpus's clearest physical comparison: cutting a tree once at the root severs its life-root, whereas chopping its branches does not (one cut at the root severs the life-root; if you chop at the branches, can you sever the life-root?). Ying'an's record says that when a blind was rolled up, “the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot” (the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot). A public exchange asks whether one who has let go at a cliff has yet severed the life-root; the answer postpones speech until the questioner's own life-root is severed. The recurring collocations thus make cutting or breaking the life-root a Chan-loaded use, distinct from the enumerated vital faculty in the second sense; the entry makes no claim about an inward meaning beyond those recorded predicates.
Senses.Note: Common forms include 'the life-root is not severed' and 'sever the life-root.' Gao-feng's question, 'a person who has completely broken through is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?' (a completely broken-through person is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?), became a repeatedly cited saying.

Occurrences.Kwic: 天下老和尚．諸上座命根。總在這裏。有僧出曰。還收得也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under Luyuan Heshang: he spreads his hand and says, 'the life-roots of all the old masters and senior monks are all here.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如人斫樹，根下一刀，則命根斷矣。汝向枝上斫，其能斷命根乎？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Hui'an Miguang's biography: 'one cut at the root severs the life-root; if you chop at the branches, can you sever it?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日見卷簾，豁然漆桶破，命根嚗地斷，便說箇頌子
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ying'an's record reports: on seeing a blind rolled up, 'the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：懸崖撒手底人命根還斷也未？師云：待闍黎命根斷即道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public question and answer in Wuyi Yuanlai's record: asked whether the life-root is severed, the master says he will speak when the questioner's is severed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大徹底人本脫生死，因什命根不斷？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Sanfeng Cang quotes Gao-feng's enduring question: 'a completely broken-through person is originally free of birth and death; why is the life-root not severed?'

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪別無奇特，祇要當人命根斷，疑情脫，千眼頓開
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address says that investigating Chan requires the person's life-root to be severed and the mass of doubt to fall away.

Senses.Explanation: In enumerative prose, the same graphs name the vital faculty as one faculty among others. The Record of the Source-Mirror says, 'among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost' (among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost). This is a different referent from the Chan idiom that masters locate, seize, and sever, so it is retained separately rather than blurred into that usage.
Senses.Note: This sense is included because it is attested within the allowlisted record, not because a Buddhist glossary controls the Chan sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如諸根中。命根為最。佛正法正行中。此心為最。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of the Source-Mirror uses the term in an explicit comparison: 'among the faculties, the vital faculty is foremost.'
